'''''Sisymbrium irio''''', '''London rocket''', is a flowering plant in the [[cabbage family]]. Its English common name originated when it flourished after the Great Fire of London in 1666, although it is not native to Britain and it does not tend to persist there.

It is native to the Middle East, north Africa and southern Europe, and which has spread widely around the world as an invasive plant of dry, disturbed land in towns, deserts and farmland. It has traditionally been used as a medicinal herb for a variety of ailments. 

==Description==
London rocket is a winter annual [[Herbaceous plant|herb]] which is very variable in size. It can grow to be a large, leafy plant as much as {{Convert|130|cm}} tall in Britain,<ref name=Sell2>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=P.D. |last2=Murrell |first2=G. |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 2 |date=2014 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=978-0-521-55336-0}}</ref> but only a small, rosette-forming one about {{Convert|10|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} tall in [[Arabian Peninsula|Arabia]],<ref name=Collenette>{{cite book |last1=Collenette |first1=Sheila |title=An Illustrated Guide to the Flowers of Saudi Arabia |date=1985 |publisher=Scorpion Publishing |location=London |isbn=0-905906-45-4}}</ref> where it is native. It has an erect, usually branched stem which is green, terete, solid and almost [[glabrousness|glabrous]], except for a smattering of soft, short hairs ({{Convert|0.5|mm|disp=or|frac=32}} long). The leaves are alternate and [[pinnation|imparipinnate]] or pinnatisect, up to {{Convert|18|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long, with one to five pairs of lateral lobes and a round or ternate terminal lobe. The petioles are up to {{Convert|6|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long, channelled and slightly decurrent down the stem, without stipules. They are finely hairy on both surfaces, uniformly green except for a pale midrib, and have a peppery flavour.<ref name="Stace">{{Cite book |last=Stace |first=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |publisher=C&M Floristics |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2 |location=Suffolk}}</ref><ref name=Rose>{{cite book |last1=Rose |first1=Francis |title=The Wild Flower Key |date=2006 |publisher=Frederick Warne |location=London|isbn=978-0-7232-5175-0}}</ref><ref name=Poland>{{cite book |last1=Poland |first1=John |last2=Clement |first2=Eric |title=The Vegetative Key to the British Flora |date=2009 |publisher=John Poland |location=Southampton |isbn=978-0-9560144-0-5}}</ref>
[[File:Sisymbrium irio Whitstable.jpg|thumb|London rocket in flower and fruit]]

The [[floral symmetry|actinomorphic]] flowers are about {{Convert|5|mm|abbr=on|frac=8}} in diameter and are arranged in racemes of 50–100 or more at the tips of the main stem and the branches. Each flower has 4 yellow petals, 4 green, finely hairy sepals which are nearly as long as the petals, and 6 stamens. The flower stalks (pedicels) are short at flowering time, creating a rather flat-topped and crowded inflorescence, but they elongate as the fruits develop, soon causing them to overtop the flowers. The fruit is a long (3–8 cm) narrow cylindrical [[silique]] which stays green when ripe and is slightly torulose (i.e. with lumps where the seeds occur, like a string of beads), and they are held at a divergent angle to the stem on the long, thin, hairy pedicels. When dried the fruit contains one row of small (about 1 mm) red oblong seeds in each of the two valves of the silique, amounting to about 100 seeds in each pod. A single plant can therefore produce many tens of thousands of seeds in total.<ref name="Sell2" /><ref name="Kim" />

=== Identification ===
[[File:Sisymbrium irio sl27.jpg|thumb|The fruiting pedicel is long and narrower than the silique]]
London rocket can easily be confused with other species of ''[[Sisymbrium]]''. Characters to look for include the compact flower head, the way the developing seedpods extend above the flowers, and the long, thin pedicels which are narrower than the fruits.<ref name="Sell2" />

==Taxonomy==
The name ''Sisymbrium irio'' was coined by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] in 1753, in his ''[[Species Plantarum]]''.<ref>Vol. 2, p. 659.</ref> Since then it has accumulated many synonyms, including ''Phryne laxata'' (by Pietro Bubani in 1901) and ''Arabis charbonnelii'' (by Augustin Léveillé in 1913), but the original name is still accepted as the correct one. A full list of synonyms is given in the [https://www.gbif.org/dataset/b6349cdd-9d7e-4b23-8c05-a231f0ffa1a0 Update on the Brassicaceae Species Checklist].<ref name=GBIF>{{cite web |last1=Global Biodiversity Information Facility |title=Sisymbrium irio L. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/3046851 |access-date=20 April 2023}}</ref>

Several subspecies and varieties have also been named over the years, but again none is currently accepted.<ref name=powo>{{cite web |last1=Plants of the World Online |title=Sisymbrium irio L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:237940-2 |access-date=20 April 2023}}</ref>

The chromosome number of London rocket is a complex subject. The [[Ploidy|diploid]] has 14 [[chromosome]]s (2n = 14), but there are triploid, tetraploid, hexaploid and octoploid "races" with 21, 28, 42 and 56 chromosomes, respectively. These races have different phenotypes and ecological adaptations, and they vary in their fertility, with the triploid being almost entirely sterile.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Khoshoo |first1=T.N. |title=Biosystematics of Sisymbrium irio complex, IX: Genome analysis |journal=J. Indian Bot. Soc. |date=1960 |volume=39 |pages=217–226 |url=http://210.212.232.211:8080/jspui/bitstream/123456789/4864/1/CMFRI-%20131%20article%2023.pdf}}</ref>

==Distribution and status==
London rocket is thought to be native in the Middle East and as far eastward as northwest India or Mongolia, and westward throughout North Africa and southern Europe. It has been introduced to North America, where it is considered something of a pest species in the southern US and Mexico, and to South America, Australasia and southern Africa. It has also spread as far east as Korea and Japan.<ref name="powo" /><ref name="GBIF" /><ref name=Kim>{{cite journal |last1=Kim |first1=Hye-Won |last2=Choi |first2=Tae-Young |last3=Son |first3=Dong Chan |last4=Jo |first4=Hyeryun |last5=Lee |first5=Soo-Rang |title=''Sisymbrium irio'' L. (Brassicaceae): a new alien plant in Korea |journal=BioInvasions Records |date=2021 |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=453–466 |doi=10.3391/bir.2021.10.2.23|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Its status internationally has not been evaluated, but it is not considered to be at risk in most countries in which it occurs, as is classified as Least Concern.<ref>{{cite web |last1=European Nature Information System |title=Sisymbrium irio L. |url=https://eunis.eea.europa.eu/species/164646 |access-date=20 April 2023}}</ref>

London rocket was introduced to Britain by the 1650s and has maintained a scattered distribution since then. It does not tend to persist in any site for long, and is even believed to have disappeared from London by the late 19th century, only to be reintroduced again in the 20th. It comes in via docks and other transport hubs, and it used to turn up in fields that had been treated with wool [[Recycled wool|shoddy]]. Overall, the population has remained more or less stable for centuries, although its transient nature means there are many more places where it used to occur than there are at any one time, leading to the mistaken impression that it is perpetually declining.<ref name=Swindells>{{cite book |last1=Swindells |first1=John |title=''Sisymbrium irio'' L. (London-rocket): its status in Britain and Ireland |date=2006 |publisher=Masters dissertation |location=University of Birmingham |url=https://archive.org/details/status-of-sisymbrium-irio}}</ref><ref name=Atlas>{{cite book |last1=Preston |first1=C.D. |last2=Pearman |first2=D.A. |last3=Dines |first3=T.D. |title=New Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |date=2002 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford}}</ref>

One country where it has recently arrived is South Korea, where it has been studied very closely. The point of arrival was the port of [[Busan]], from where it spread {{Convert|1.5|km|4=1}} along a roadside over a 10 year period. It is currently considered to be established but not invasive.<ref name="Kim" />

==Habitat and ecology==
The [http://dbif.brc.ac.uk/hostsresults.aspx?hostid=5260 Database of Insects and their Food Plants] lists just two species that make use of London rocket: ''Ceutorhynchus hirtulus'' is a weevil that lives in the soil and creates stem galls for it larvae,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Plant Parasites of Europe |title=Ceutorhynchus hirtulus Germar, 1824 |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/parasites/animalia/arthropoda/insecta/coleoptera/polyphaga/cucujiformia/curculionoidea/curculionidae/conoderinae/ceutorhynchitae/ceutorhynchini/ceutorhynchus/ceutorhynchus-hirtulus/ |access-date=23 April 2023}}</ref> whereas [[cabbage looper]] moth larvae eat the leaves of this and many other species in the cabbage family.

This species is considered a [[noxious weed|weed]] in the [[Southwestern United States]] and other regions where it has been introduced.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hennessy-Fiske |first=Molly |date=2019-03-11 |title=Naturalists scour border to draw attention to habitat, not migrant crisis |url=https://www.latimes.com/nation/la-na-arizona-border-bioblitz-20190311-story.html |access-date=2019-03-12 |website=[[Los Angeles Times]]}}</ref>

==History==
The first published record of this species in Britain was by [[Christopher Merret]] in 1666, who described ''Irio laevis'' as being "almost everywhere in the suburbs of London on walls and near ditches".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Merrett |first1=Cristopher |url=https://archive.org/details/b30341085/page/66/ |title=Pinax Rerum Naturalium Britannicarum |date=1666 |location=London |page=66 |quote=ubique fere in suburbiis Lond. supra muros et juxta fossas}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Clarke |first1=W.A. |title=First Records of British Flowering Plants |date=1900 |publisher=West, Newman & Co. |location=London}}</ref> It had, however, been noticed at least a decade earlier: William How (1620–1656) had annotated his own copy of his book ''Phytologia Britannica'' (1650) with the comment "near White Chappel east from Aldgate, London"; a discovery he attributed to [[John Goodyer]].<ref name="Swindells" />

The term "London" in the [[common name]] "London rocket" allegedly comes from its abundance after the [[Great Fire of London]] in 1666.<ref>{{cite book|author1=A.R. Clapham |author2=E.F. Warburg |author3=T.G. Tutin |title=Flora of the British Isles|url=https://archive.org/details/excursionfloraof0000clap |url-access=registration |year=1968 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=9780521046565 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://daily.jstor.org/plant-of-the-month-london-rocket/|work=[[JSTOR#Content|JSTOR Daily]]|title=Plant of the Month: London Rocket|first=Beth|last=Kidd|date=March 30, 2023|access-date=April 7, 2023}}</ref> [[Robert Morison]], the physician to King Charles II, attributed their appearance to [[spontaneous generation]] when he observed that “these hot bitter plants with four petals and pods were produced spontaneously without seed by the ashes of the fire mixed with salt and lime.”<ref name="Weeds">{{Cite book |last=Mabey |first=Richard |author-link=Richard Mabey |title=Weeds: In Defence of Nature's Most Unloved Plants |date=June 28, 2011 |publisher=[[Ecco Press]] |isbn=978-0062065452 |pages=209 |chapter=Chapter 10 French Willow}}</ref> By contrast, Dr E.J. Salisbury, in his study of the bombsites of London after [[the Blitz]] in 1940, "failed to find a single specimen, nor has any other reliable observer reported it".<ref>{{cite book |last=Fitter |first=R. S. R. |date=1945 |title= London's Natural History |url=https://archive.org/details/londonsnaturalhi00fitt|url-access=registration |location=London |publisher=Collins |page=[https://archive.org/details/londonsnaturalhi00fitt/page/231 231] |isbn=1-870630-69-6}}</ref><ref>{{google books|id=9o7rq6WnSXEC|page=11|title=The Ecology of Transportation}}</ref>

The term "Rocket" in the common name appears to be derived from the old Latin term "eruca" applied to several loosely related plants in the cabbage family.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mabey |first=Richard |title=Weeds: In Defense of Nature's Most Unloved Plants |date=2010 |publisher=HarperCollins |isbn=978-0-06-206545-2 |edition=1st U.S. |location=New York, NY |page=[https://archive.org/details/weedsindefenseof0000mabe/page/208 209] |ol=OL25004437M}}</ref>

==Uses==
In desert regions of Arabia and Egypt, London rocket is considered an important source of fodder for livestock.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shehata |first1=H.F.S. |title=Ecology and nutritive status of ''Sisymbrium irio'' L. in the Nile Delta, Egypt |journal=Egypt. J. Exp. Biol. (Bot.) |date=2014 |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=127–142 |url=http://www.egyseb.net/fulltext/15-1429985439.pdf}}</ref>

The leaves, seeds, and flowers are edible to humans, with a spicy flavor similar to cultivated [[Eruca sativa|rocket]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://savorthesouthwest.blog/tag/edible-weeds/|title=edible weeds {{!}} Savor the Southwest|website=savorthesouthwest.blog|date=14 February 2014 |language=en|access-date=2018-11-18}}</ref> London rocket is used in the [[Middle East]] to treat coughs and chest congestion, to relieve [[rheumatism]], to detoxify the liver and spleen, and to reduce swelling and clean wounds.<ref>Lev, Efraima (2003) "''Sisymbrium irio''" ''Medicinal substances in Jerusalem from early times to the present day'' Archaeopress, Oxford, UK, p. 62, {{ISBN|978-1-84171-490-5}}</ref>

The [[Bedouin]] of the [[Sinai Peninsula]] and the [[Negev]] desert reportedly used the leaf of London rocket as a tobacco substitute, and a recent study of the alkaloid content of desert-grown plants in Iraq found a high concentration of [[nicotine]] in extracts of the aerial parts of this plant.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bailey |first1=C. |last2=Danin |first2=A. |title=Bedouin Plant Utilization in Sinai and the Negev |journal=Economic Botany |date=1981 |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=145–162 |doi=10.1007/BF02858682 |jstor=4254272 |s2cid=27839209 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4254272|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alsaffar |first1=A.F |last2=Abbas |first2=I.S. |last3=Dawood |first3=A.H. |title=Investigation of the Main Alkaloid of London Rocket (Sisymbrium irio L) as a Wild Medicinal Plant Grown in Iraq |journal=Int. J. Pharm. Sci. Rev. Res. |date=2016 |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=279–281 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/306159100}}</ref> 

The cured pods can be placed in a basket with live coals and shaken until the pods are parched, then ground into meal and made into soup or stew.<ref>Warnock, Barton H. (1977) "Wildflowers of the Davis Mountains and the Marathon Basin, Texas", p. 111</ref>
